sources.title: Online habits and well-being
sources.population: Almost 280,000 young people aged 11, 13 and 15 in 44 countries and regions in Europe, central Asia and Canada; surveyed in 2022.
sources.finding: The survey found signs of problematic social media use in 11% of respondents. Heavy use without those problems was also associated with stronger peer support.
sources.limit: A population survey does not diagnose an individual or establish a universal safe number of minutes. Associations do not prove that one habit caused an outcome.
sources.prompt: What is the habit helping you do, and what is it getting in the way of?

sources.title: Judging information before using it
sources.population: General media and information literacy guidance for people engaging with information online.
sources.finding: UNESCO describes media literacy as the skills needed to engage critically with information and navigate digital environments safely.
sources.limit: This is educational guidance, not an experiment measuring how much a particular checking routine improves accuracy.
sources.prompt: Who made the claim, what original evidence supports it, and what context is missing?

sources.title: Keeping personal information private
sources.publisher: Government of Canada · Get Cyber Safe
sources.population: General guidance for people using online accounts; not a participant study.
sources.finding: Get Cyber Safe recommends unique account passwords and multi-factor authentication, and asks users to take precautions before posting on social media.
sources.limit: These steps reduce particular exposures. They cannot guarantee account security or remove information that others have already copied.
sources.prompt: Could a post or prompt reveal more about you or someone else than you intended?

sources.title: Human judgment when using generative AI
sources.publisher: UNESCO · Fengchun Miao and Wayne Holmes
sources.population: Global guidance for education and research, including educators and policy-makers.
sources.finding: UNESCO's guidance emphasizes human agency, data privacy, and educational validation when using generative AI.
sources.limit: Policy guidance is not a test of a specific AI tool. A polished answer still needs evidence appropriate to the task.
sources.prompt: What will you verify yourself, and what information should stay out of the prompt?

topics.label: Screen time & attention
topics.description: Look at when and why you use a screen, and what you want that time to do.
risks: Losing time intended for another activity

example.observation: I plan to scroll for ten minutes, then keep going for about an hour.
example.context: After homework, while I am deciding what to do next.
example.notice: I enjoy catching up, but I sometimes postpone the drawing I wanted to finish.
example.evidenceResponse: The WHO survey gives context, but it cannot tell me whether my own sixty minutes are a problem. I need to observe what gets displaced.
example.risk: Losing time intended for another activity
example.benefit: Keeping up with friends and discovering art.
example.change: Set aside twenty minutes for scrolling, then put my phone away and start drawing.
example.check: Note on three evenings whether I started drawing when I planned to.

topics.label: Social media & privacy
topics.description: Consider the audience for a post and the details it reveals.
risks: Posting to a wider audience than intended

example.observation: I share photos from a club meeting before checking what is in the background.
example.context: Posting a story so friends can see what our group is doing.
example.notice: A noticeboard in one photo includes a member's contact details.
example.evidenceResponse: Canadian security guidance supports checking personal details before posting. It cannot promise that a deleted post disappears from every copy.
example.benefit: Celebrating our club and staying connected.
example.change: Check the background and ask people pictured before posting the next club photo.
example.check: Use a brief permission and background check for my next three posts.

topics.label: News & information
topics.description: Trace an appealing claim to its source before sharing it.
risks: Mistaking an old claim for current news

example.observation: I almost share a viral post saying our city's buses will be free next month.
example.context: A friend shares a cropped screenshot in a group chat.
example.notice: The screenshot has no date or link to an official announcement.
example.evidenceResponse: Media literacy guidance helps me ask for the original source and context. Neither source here verifies this fictional bus claim.
example.benefit: Helping friends find useful transport information.
example.change: Find a dated transit-agency announcement before forwarding the claim. If I cannot verify it, say that clearly.
example.check: For the next three news posts I consider sharing, record whether I found an original source.

topics.label: AI-assisted tools
topics.description: Decide what the tool can help with and what you need to check yourself.
risks: Including private information in a prompt
Skipping my own learning or task rules

example.observation: I use an AI summary as a starting point without checking its references.
example.context: Learning about a topic for a project where AI assistance is permitted.
example.notice: The summary sounds clear, but I cannot yet explain where its main claim came from.
example.evidenceResponse: UNESCO recommends human agency and educational validation. That is a reason to check the answer, not evidence that this particular summary is correct.
example.benefit: Getting a starting explanation and questions to investigate.
example.change: Check the main claim against an original source and write an explanation in my own words.
example.check: Before using my next AI summary, note the original source and what I corrected.
